question: Which statement best describes String literal types?
options: Literals aren't limited to strings. A number literal like 200 or a boolean literal like true is also a type with exactly one value. These appear in unions such as HTTP status codes (200 | 404 | 500) or precise flag types.

Adding as const tells TypeScript to infer the narrowest, immutable type: the literal itself rather than the widened base type. const dir = 'left' as const has type 'left', not string. Applied to objects/arrays it makes them deeply readonly with literal members.

The most common and useful form: a union of literal values defines a closed set of allowed inputs. type Size = 'sm' | 'md' | 'lg' lets the compiler reject any other string and provide autocomplete for the three valid options — far safer than typing it as string.

A string literal type is a type whose only allowed value is one specific string. let dir: 'left' accepts only the string 'left' — anything else is a compile error. On its own a single literal is rarely useful; its power shows in unions.
